passage:
People ask me, "Gargi, how did you know?" I didn't know. I noticed. Farida used to be first to reply in our group chat, and then she stopped. Three Friday dinners in a row her seat stayed empty and I got "busy, next time."
At first I sent long worried messages and got nothing back. So I changed. I sent a photo of the dosa place she likes with "No need to reply, thinking of you." Then a voice note about my own terrible week.
A fortnight later: "Sorry I went quiet. Coffee?" Sitting there, she said things had felt heavy for a while. I said that if it stays heavy, someone trained to help could be worth trying, and I'd come along to the first visit if she wanted. I didn't push. I just kept leaving the door ajar.

qa.q: How many Friday dinners did Farida's seat stay empty?
qa.a: Three Friday dinners in a row.

qa.q: What did Gargi feel and think about Farida going quiet?
qa.a: Gargi noticed and worried, but was not sure why. At first Gargi pushed with long messages, then softened when nothing came back.

qa.q: What change of approach did Gargi make when the long messages got no reply?
qa.a: Gargi sent a photo of the dosa place with a note saying no need to reply, and then a voice note about Gargi's own week.

qa.q: What might Farida have felt when the short, low-pressure messages arrived?
qa.a: She may have felt remembered without being pressured, which could be why she replied later and said things had felt heavy.

grounding: A friend notices someone slowly declining invitations and reaches out gently and without pressure.

passage:
I'm Aadhya, and I share the pantry table with Joseph. He used to eat lunch with us, then started saying "I'll skip today," then stopped coming to the Friday quiz, and lately his replies on our team chat arrive a day late and one line long. I can't tell why, and it might just be a busy stretch. But nobody had checked in, so I left a mug of tea at his desk with a note: "No need to talk. The pantry table's yours whenever."
He didn't answer for two days. Then he came and sat, saying little. I told him I'd noticed he had gone quiet and that I was around, and that if things felt too heavy, there are people whose job is to help, and I could sit with him while he called. He nodded. He looked tired but not unfriendly.

qa.q: What did Aadhya leave at Joseph's desk?
qa.a: A mug of tea with a note.

qa.q: What is Aadhya feeling about Joseph's withdrawal?
qa.a: Aadhya is concerned but careful. Aadhya cannot tell why Joseph has gone quiet and admits it might be a busy stretch.

qa.q: What did Aadhya do to reach out without pressure?
qa.a: Aadhya left tea and a note saying no need to talk, then later said Aadhya was around and offered to sit with Joseph while he called someone who helps.

qa.q: How might Joseph feel when he sees the mug and the note?
qa.a: Possibly tired and unsure, but not pressured. He takes two days, then comes and sits, which suggests the note made it feel safe.

grounding: A colleague notices someone slowly withdrawing and reaches out gently with low-pressure invitations.

passage:
June. Gargi noticed Keerthana skip the Friday dinner again, with a thumbs-up and "next time!" It was the third "next time" in a row.
August. Keerthana's replies had shrunk to single words. When Gargi called, it rang out. Her photos had stopped. Gargi almost let it go; everyone was busy. Instead she sent a message: "No need to reply. Just thinking of you. Chai on Sunday if you feel like it, my place, no plans."
September. On Sunday Keerthana turned up, hair uncombed, and sat on Gargi's floor for two hours. At first she said little. Then: "I've been in a bad patch since the job ended. I didn't want to be a downer." Gargi made more chai. Before Keerthana left, they set another Sunday, and Keerthana said she'd look for a counsellor.

qa.q: What did Gargi offer in the August message?
qa.a: Chai on Sunday at Gargi's place, with no plans and no need to reply.

qa.q: What made Gargi decide not to let it go in August?
qa.a: Gargi felt worried, noticing single-word replies, unanswered calls and stopped photos after three "next time"s.

qa.q: Why did Gargi's message work?
qa.a: It was gentle and low-pressure, asking for nothing and offering an easy, open invitation.

qa.q: Why had Keerthana been pulling away?
qa.a: Keerthana was in a bad patch since the job ended and didn't want to be a downer.

grounding: Shows a friend noticing someone slowly declining invitations and replying less, and reaching out gently.

passage:
Saurabh, sit. You say your friend Kunal has stopped answering? Let me tell you about Leela. When I was twenty-four, teaching in Pune, Leela and I shared everything. Then her father died, and slowly she stopped coming to the Sunday market with us. First she said she was tired. Then she said nothing.
I told myself she wanted space. For two months I waited. That was my mistake.
One evening I just went to her door with a packet of her favourite jalebis. I didn't ask questions. I said, "I'm here for an hour, if you want company." She opened the door. We sat and ate and hardly talked. I went back every Thursday. Months later she told me those Thursdays were the only thing she looked forward to.
So, Saurabh, don't wait two months like your Irawati Aaji did.

qa.q: What did Irawati bring to Leela's door?
qa.a: A packet of Leela's favourite jalebis.

qa.q: How does Irawati now feel about those two months of waiting?
qa.a: Irawati feels regretful, calling the two months of waiting a mistake.

qa.q: Which choice in the story made the difference for Leela?
qa.a: Going to Leela's door with jalebis and a no-questions offer of company, then returning every Thursday.

qa.q: What did the Thursday visits mean to Leela?
qa.a: They were the only thing Leela looked forward to during that time.

grounding: Shows a friend noticing someone slowly withdrawing after a loss, and gentle, low-pressure visits making a difference.

passage:
Urmila was working night shifts at the hospital in Nagpur, and her friend Sahil lived four hundred kilometres away in Indore. Their weekly calls had slipped to monthly, then to nothing. Lately his replies in the group chat were just a heart, if anything. He had skipped the online quiz night three times.
Urmila had no time to visit, and she was usually asleep when others were awake. But on a slow night at 4 am she recorded a short voice note: "No need to reply. I miss your terrible jokes. I'll send you one voice note every Sunday, even if you don't answer."
She kept it up for five Sundays. On the sixth, a reply came: "Sorry I went quiet. Things have been heavy. Can we talk on your day off?" Urmila set an alarm for the afternoon so she wouldn't sleep through it.

qa.q: How many Sundays did Urmila send voice notes before Sahil replied?
qa.a: Five Sundays; the reply came on the sixth.

qa.q: What might Urmila have been feeling when she recorded the first voice note?
qa.a: Urmila was probably worried about Sahil and missed him, noticing the single hearts, the skipped quiz nights and the silence.

qa.q: Why did voice notes suit this situation?
qa.a: They were low-pressure and fit Urmila's night shifts and the distance, asking for no reply while showing steady care.

qa.q: What was it like for Sahil to receive them?
qa.a: Sahil was going through a heavy time, and the steady notes seem to have made it easier to reach back and ask to talk.

grounding: Shows a friend noticing someone replying less and skipping plans, and reaching out in a gentle, low-pressure way.

passage:
In the Bengaluru office canteen, Trisha realised it had been six weeks since Deepika had come for Friday dinner. First it was "tired". Then "work". Then just a thumbs-up and no reply. Her messages, once long and full of jokes, were now one word.
Trisha remembered Deepika saying, months ago, that she liked her own company. That was true. But this felt different, like a slow fading.
She didn't want to push or make a big scene. So she texted: "No plan, no pressure. I'm going to buy flowers at the market on Sunday morning. Want to walk with me? Even ten minutes."
No reply that day. Trisha felt the urge to send a second, worried message, and didn't.
Sunday morning, 8:10: "ok. ten minutes."
They walked for an hour. Deepika said very little at first. Near the end she said, "I don't know why I've been hiding. Thanks for not giving up."

qa.q: How long had it been since Deepika came for Friday dinner?
qa.a: It had been six weeks.

qa.q: What was Trisha feeling as Deepika's replies shrank?
qa.a: Trisha felt worried and uneasy, sensing this was not ordinary time alone but a slow fading.

qa.q: Which of Trisha's choices helped, and why?
qa.a: She reached out gently with a short, low-pressure invitation and didn't flood Deepika with worried messages, which made it easy to say yes.

qa.q: How did Deepika feel by the end of the walk?
qa.a: Deepika felt grateful and a little relieved, thanking Trisha for not giving up on her.

grounding: A friend notices someone slowly declining invitations and reaches out gently, since withdrawal grows quietly when nobody checks.
